title: Leveraging quantum computing business applications: a B-SLR approach and future research directions
abstract_summary: This review combines a PRISMA-compliant systematic literature review with bibliometric analysis to synthesize business applications of quantum computing across domains such as optimization, cryptography/cybersecurity, machine learning, finance, supply chain, healthcare, and materials design. It highlights practical constraints (NISQ vs fault-tolerant distinction, hardware readiness, qubit capacity, costs, skills, and governance), advocates hybrid quantum–classical implementation and sector-specific readiness, and proposes the QCSA framework plus a research and policy agenda to guide organizational adoption and future studies.
methodology_description: The study used a Bibliometric-Systematic Literature Review (B-SLR) approach integrating a PRISMA-compliant systematic review with quantitative bibliometric mapping. Data were collected exclusively from the Scopus database for peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2015 and 2025. The lead author conducted the initial database search and screening; a co-author independently reviewed the search strategy and screening decisions, and discrepancies were resolved by discussion and consensus. The Boolean search string was: "quantum" AND "computing" AND "business" AND "applications". Initial retrieval returned 166 records; results were filtered by document type (articles only), source type (journals), language (English), publication stage (final), and subject areas (Business, Management & Accounting; Economics, Econometrics & Finance; Decision Sciences; Computer Science). Title/abstract screening removed studies focused purely on quantum physics, hardware engineering, or purely technical algorithms without business relevance. After full-text eligibility screening, 33 peer-reviewed journal articles met inclusion criteria and were retained. Bibliometric analyses (using Scopus metadata) included publication trends, citation patterns, leading authors and affiliations, country citation impact, co-authorship and co-occurrence keyword analyses, co-word network metrics (betweenness, closeness, PageRank), word cloud generation, and thematic mapping (centrality vs. density). A qualitative systematic synthesis of the included articles then evaluated application domains, technological requirements (distinguishing NISQ vs. fault-tolerant), organizational readiness, barriers, and strategic implications, and mapped findings to theoretical perspectives (e.g., TOE, RBV, Diffusion of Innovations). The study produced PRISMA flow documentation and multiple bibliometric visualisations (word cloud, co-word table, thematic map).

key_findings: [supported] The distinction between NISQ-era (noisy intermediate-scale) devices and fault-tolerant quantum computers is the dominant determinant of near-term business feasibility for quantum applications.

[supported] Near-term value is expected primarily from hybrid quantum–classical configurations and application-specific algorithms that can operate within NISQ constraints (shallow circuits, error mitigation, classical loops).
[supported] Pure end-to-end quantum solutions in real-world business contexts are currently absent in the reviewed literature; hybrid architectures dominate reported application pathways.

[supported] Quantum readiness is sector-specific: cybersecurity/post-quantum cryptography and certain financial optimization use-cases are relatively high priority, while pharmaceuticals, materials, and many high‑accuracy quantum-chemistry tasks require fault-tolerant hardware and are longer-term.

[supported] Organizations face recurring barriers to adoption: hardware maturity (qubit count, error rates), cost (development and operation), talent shortages, integration complexity with classical systems, and lack of clear regulation/standards.

[supported] Bibliometric analysis (Scopus-based) shows a clear publication surge from ~2020 onward, concentration in technical journals (e.g., Quantum Information Processing), and geographically diverse contributions with high citation activity from China, India and the USA.

[supported] The authors synthesized co-word/clustering analyses showing research themes split between core theory/physics (quantum theory, entanglement, quantum chemistry) and application-oriented clusters (cryptography, quantum optics, IoT, AI).
[supported] Preparing for post-quantum cryptography (migration planning, standards) is an urgent, actionable priority called out in the literature and policy reports cited.

[speculative] The authors propose the Quantum Computing Strategic Alignment (QCSA) framework to position applications by Technological Readiness and Organizational Capability with Strategic Value as an overlay (Immediate Action, Capability Accumulation, Structured Experimentation, Observation zones).

[speculative] The Resource-Based View implication that early quantum capabilities will likely yield transient (not sustained) competitive advantage under NISQ conditions (i.e., advantages are time-dependent and contingent).

[speculative] Managerial recommendations (treat quantum as capability-building, prioritize hybrid experiments, invest in workforce and governance, integrate PQC planning) are forward-looking prescriptions rather than empirically validated interventions.

[speculative] Key future research gaps identified: empirical, sector-specific case studies; longitudinal studies of firm adoption; standardized benchmarking including total cost of ownership; engineering of hybrid middleware and orchestration; life‑cycle/environmental assessments; and workforce training models.

[supported] Methodological limitation: the review used Scopus-indexed, peer‑reviewed journal articles (2015–2025), English only; final systematic screen retained 33 articles for in-depth analysis (PRISMA-guided).
results_summary: The review combines bibliometric mapping and a PRISMA-style systematic synthesis of Scopus-indexed literature (2015–2025) to conclude that, in the near term, practical business value from quantum computing will come via hybrid quantum–classical approaches and NISQ-compatible algorithms rather than from fault-tolerant, large‑scale quantum machines. Readiness and strategic value are sector-dependent (with cybersecurity and some financial applications prioritized), and adoption is constrained by hardware, cost, skills, integration complexity, and regulation. The authors introduce a Quantum Computing Strategic Alignment (QCSA) framework to help organizations map technological readiness against internal capabilities and strategic importance and outline a research agenda emphasizing empirical case studies, hybrid system engineering, standardized benchmarks, and policy/ethical work.

quantum_advantage_detail: The review finds no demonstrated, general-purpose quantum advantage in business/financial services to date; near-term advantages are expected to be narrow, application-specific, and contingent on hybrid quantum–classical methods (NISQ-compatible). Large-scale, broadly transformative quantum advantage requiring fault tolerance remains theoretical/long-term and unproven in commercial contexts.
limitations: Study restricted to peer-reviewed journal articles indexed in Scopus published between 2015–2025 (English only), excluding conference papers, books, technical reports, white papers, and non-English sources.
Conclusions are time-bound and may not reflect the very latest technological or regulatory developments in a fast-moving field.
Reliance on secondary literature prevented empirical evaluation of actual performance outcomes, real-world organizational adoption, and return-on-investment (ROI).
[inferred] Small final sample (33 included articles) may limit representativeness and the generalizability of bibliometric and qualitative conclusions.
[inferred] Using Scopus as the sole source may introduce disciplinary and publication-type bias and underrepresent industry/gray literature and regional publications.
